prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, based on reversible-terminator nucleotide chemistry and fluorescent detection on surface-immobilised templates.

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from biomolecular phase separation (B029) to massively parallel sequencing by synthesis (B017), credited to Balasubramanian and Klenerman. The round-1 exchange showed that B017 is the only candidate that five members independently place first, from different scientific viewpoints, and no one argues it is immature or scientifically thin. That is not a vote count substituting for judgment: I weighed it because the substantive case holds up. Reversible-terminator nucleotides, fluorescent labelling and single-molecule templates on a surface are molecular design that turned a chemical reaction into a parallel digital readout, with two decades of independent confirmation and consequences that are demonstrated rather than anticipated. As a physical chemist I also note that making this work depends on surface chemistry, controlled reaction kinetics on immobilised molecules and optical readout, which is chemistry in the strict sense and not only a biological tool. I keep the Cambridge pair because they conceived and integrated the chemistry and detection. I would not add Mayer on the evidence in front of us: clonal amplification on a surface is a real contribution, but the committee has no verified priority record, and a citation that names clusters while excluding him would read as arbitrary, so my citation is worded around the terminator chemistry.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem remains real: Ju (terminator chemistry), Rothberg (pyrosequencing and semiconductor sequencing) and Mayer (clonal colonies) have genuine claims, and a Cambridge-pair citation leaves out the 454 lineage entirely. Sanger and Gilbert were recognised in 1980, so a sceptic can call this a scale-up of a recognised capability rather than a new principle, and part of the impact belongs to physiology or medicine. My own previous first choice, B029, is a stronger new concept of molecular organisation but remains weaker than B017 on in vivo maturity and on demonstrated consequence, and a three-name cut excludes Pappu and Mittag.

responses.point: Aili prefers the Balasubramanian and Klenerman pair as the cleanest B017 configuration and wants the citation to say clearly that this is chemistry, while ranking condensates fourth because of limited maturity.
responses.response: I now agree with her on both points. I still think the chemistry-versus-biology worry about condensates is overstated, since the explanatory content is phase behaviour and multivalency, but her maturity point about the in vivo status is fair and I concede it. On B017 I adopt the pair and a citation that names the reversible-terminator chemistry and surface-bound templates, so that the recognised discovery is plainly chemistry. I differ slightly on wording: I would leave 'clonally amplified clusters' out, because it implicitly credits the Mayer contribution while the laureate list excludes him.

responses.point: Aqvist proposes adding Pascal Mayer as third laureate for clonal clustering, but names the Cambridge pair alone as the cleaner fallback if no defensible third name can be agreed.
responses.response: I take his argument seriously, because surface-bound clusters are what made the chemistry scale, and from a surface-chemistry viewpoint it is a real physical-chemical step. But he and Chabes both say priority has not been verified, and he himself accepts that Ju and Rothberg would then have comparable claims to a third seat. Adding Mayer cannot be defended better than adding either of them, so I take his own fallback, the pair alone. If the committee's expert reports establish that the cluster concept was decisive and independent, I would revisit this, but I will not assume it.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, moved from perovskites to B017 with Balasubramanian, Klenerman and Mayer, and wanted maturity settled before backing condensates, while acknowledging that a citation which excludes 454 may look arbitrary.
responses.response: His reservation on condensates is accepted: the question of which cellular assemblies are genuine phases and which are artefacts of overexpression is not settled, and a prize now would risk endorsing the concept too broadly. On the arbitrariness concern for 454, I think the answer is to word the citation around the specific chemistry, reversible-terminator sequencing on immobilised templates, so that it describes what was recognised and does not claim to define massively parallel sequencing as a whole. That makes the exclusion of pyrosequencing a statement about which chemistry is credited, not a verdict on other contributors. I differ from him on Mayer, as above.

responses.point: Somfai prefers Pd-catalysed C-N coupling by Buchwald and Hartwig for its clean two-person attribution and distinctness from the 2010 prize, and says a Cambridge-pair B017 is the strongest version and could be his second choice.
responses.response: I agree that his attribution is the cleanest on the list, and that is why B017 with the pair is the closest comparison. Where I weigh differently is breadth: B017 extends beyond synthetic chemistry into essentially every field of molecular life science, whereas C-N coupling, though a mature and widely used method, is a refinement within a framework recognised in 2010. I also note that both of us accept the other as a viable prize, so the committee has a workable path with a two-name B017 and no second part. I would not add B048 as a second part, since the two have no joint motivation and the three-person cap would be strained.

uncertainties: Whether the committee's expert material establishes that Mayer's clonal-cluster concept was independent and decisive, which would change my view on a third laureate.
Whether a citation can be worded so that the exclusion of Ju and the 454 lineage reads as a statement about the credited chemistry and not as an arbitrary judgment.
How the committee weighs the 1980 sequencing prize against the new chemistry, and whether this is regarded as a new chemical capability or a scale-up.
Whether B029 should be revisited in a few years once the in vivo status of condensates and the position of Pappu and Mittag are clearer.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B017 or its candidates is apparent from my profile. My earlier first choice B029 and my alternative B067 (lipid nanoparticles) are close to my own research on lipid self-assembly and membranes, which I flag as scientific proximity only, with no personal or institutional link to the named candidates. I sit with Lund colleagues Linke and Somfai, which is not a conflict for these candidates. No recusal is needed.
